author: Claude (English teacher role)
basis: Replaces the original B2 column of sheet 'SDG 13-1', which read at FK 17.8 with 38% long words (journal prose) and could not be said in 20 seconds. This version keeps a genuine B2 register — concession, nominalisation, hedging, academic collocation — inside the speaking limit. Facts unchanged. Band: 34-43 words, 14-20 words per sentence, FK 11-15.

slides.1: Have you noticed our summers becoming steadily longer and more intense? This is not simply an impression: the planet is in a genuine climate crisis, and melting ice remains an urgent warning we can no longer ignore.
slides.2: What exactly does SDG 13 demand of us as a country? It is an international call for climate action, requiring every nation to reduce carbon emissions and strengthen disaster resilience before rising temperatures damage our cities permanently.
slides.3: Consider Taiwan's particular position. As a densely populated island with limited land, we are highly exposed to typhoons and rising sea levels, while our advanced manufacturing sector consumes an enormous amount of electricity daily.
slides.4: Recent measurements show that Taiwan is warming faster than the global average, disrupting agricultural yields and freshwater supply alike. Without rapid intervention, today's record heatwaves will gradually become an unwelcome permanent baseline for everyone.
slides.5: Our central difficulty is a continued reliance on imported coal and natural gas, while the semiconductor industry, often called our Silicon Shield, requires absolutely uninterrupted power. Economic strength and deep emission cuts therefore appear to conflict.
slides.6: We should confront several uncomfortable questions honestly rather than postpone them. Is an energy-intensive lifestyle sustainable in the long term, and can the shift toward renewables outpace the ecological damage we cause?
slides.7: There has nevertheless been genuine progress worth recognising. Taiwan enacted the Climate Change Response Act, writing Net Zero by 2050 into law, while a national carbon fee now makes heavy polluters pay directly for their emissions.
slides.8: The landscape itself is being transformed before our eyes. Offshore wind farms across the Taiwan Strait demonstrate how quickly renewable capacity can scale, and rooftop solar keeps expanding across schools, factories and public buildings.
slides.9: Public engagement remains strong, since citizens recycle carefully and rely heavily on public transport systems. Even so, individual habits alone cannot deliver climate stability; only systemic reform actually moves national emissions downward.
slides.10: How might technology accelerate this transition further? Taiwan is developing smart grids that use artificial intelligence to balance supply and demand, which reduces waste and raises the efficiency of the entire national power system.
slides.11: Carbon capture represents another promising frontier for our engineers. They intercept carbon dioxide at industrial chimneys before it enters the atmosphere and store it underground, allowing manufacturing and environmental protection to coexist.
slides.12: In urban mobility, Taiwan's swappable-battery electric scooters have become internationally recognised. This locally developed innovation reduces air and noise pollution in dense cities, and it offers a practical template other economies can adopt.
slides.13: Decarbonisation nevertheless creates real economic friction for smaller companies, because green technology demands heavy investment that they may struggle to afford. The transition must therefore be designed so that vulnerable communities are not penalised.
slides.14: Energy security remains genuinely contested in Taiwan. Precision industry requires absolutely stable power, yet solar and wind generation are intermittent, so choosing between expanded natural gas and nuclear energy stays politically painful.
slides.15: Climate disruption ignores national borders, which means that our response has to be international in scope. Taiwan holds green technology worth sharing, although diplomatic constraints continue to complicate genuine cooperation with partner countries.
slides.16: Finally, vigilance matters a great deal here. Greenwashing allows companies to claim environmental credit without meaningful change, so informed citizens should demand verified data and hold industry and government to the 2050 commitment.
slides.17: To summarise, Taiwan is moving along the right trajectory, supported by new legislation, expanding wind capacity and increasingly intelligent energy systems. The shift from a carbon-heavy economy to a green one is difficult but entirely necessary.
slides.18: Why should any of this concern you directly? Because your generation will supply the scientists and policymakers who engineer better solutions, and because public opinion shifts noticeably when informed students decide to speak up.
slides.19: Rather than feeling paralysed by the scale of this crisis, allow it to sharpen your ambition instead. Taiwan has the talent and the determination to build a country where clean air is entirely normal.
slides.20: The clock is ticking and the planet demands decisive action, so will you simply observe this transition or help engineer it? Taiwan is ready to deliver SDG 13, and so am I. Let us begin now.
